questions.stem: Why is a position fixed from radar ranges to two or more objects preferred to a fix from radar bearings?
options: Radar ranges are more accurate than radar bearings
Radar bearings cannot be read on the screen
Range arcs need no chart
Ranges are always read instantly
questions.explanation: Ranges are timing measurements and are accurate, while bearings depend on beam width and are good to only a few degrees. A range fix is therefore more accurate than a bearing fix.

questions.stem: How is a radar range plotted on the chart as a position line?
options: Draw a straight line from the object at the radar's bearing and ignore the range
Draw a line parallel to the coast at the range
Plot the range along the ship's course line
Set dividers to the range and swing an arc from the charted object; the ship is somewhere on the arc
questions.explanation: A range from an object puts the ship on a circle around it, so an arc is drawn from the object's charted position using the range. A second arc crosses the first at the fix.

questions.stem: For a fix from two range arcs, what angle between the two objects (as seen from the ship) gives the best result?
options: About 5 degrees
About 20 degrees
About 90 degrees
About 45 degrees
questions.explanation: The best angle of cut is close to 90 degrees. When the objects are nearly in line the arcs cross at a shallow angle and a small range error moves the fix a long way. At 45 degrees the fix is still stretched.

questions.stem: Two range arcs cross at two points, one on the water you expect and one on the far side of the coast. How do you pick the right one?
options: Always take the point nearer the shore
Use the DR position, a bearing or the depth to decide, never just the one that looks safer
Always take the point nearer the larger object
Take the point nearer the bottom of the chart
questions.explanation: Two circles meet at two points, so the extra information has to choose. Picking the 'safer-looking' point is a way to hide an error.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness of a quick fix from the range and bearing of one object?
options: It relies on identifying the right object and on a bearing that is only good to a few degrees
It cannot be plotted on a paper chart
It needs a stabilised radar and a gyro-compass
It always puts the ship on the wrong side of the object
questions.explanation: One echo gives both numbers, which is fast, but any wrong identification or bearing error goes straight into the position. Confirm with depth or DR when you can.

questions.stem: A radar bearing is 4 degrees in error on an object 5.0 nm away. About what position error results?
options: About 0.04 nm
About 1.0 nm
About 5.0 nm
About 0.35 nm sideways
questions.explanation: Sideways error is about range × tan(error) = 5.0 × tan 4° = 5.0 × 0.0699 = 0.35 nm, roughly 650 m. A small angle becomes a large distance at long range.

questions.stem: A tangent bearing is taken to the edge of a steep-sided island. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It is the most accurate, because tangents are exactly 90 degrees to the track
It needs no correction because radar bearings are always centre-of-target
It is among the least accurate radar fixes, because the beam width pushes the echo's edge out and must be allowed for
It is accurate only in rain
questions.explanation: Because the beam has width, the echo's edge is pushed out by about half the beam width, so right-hand tangents are decreased and left-hand tangents increased. It is one of the least accurate radar fixes; confirm it with a range.

questions.stem: Why must you identify an object positively before using its radar range in a fix?
options: Because radar always paints the true coastline exactly
Radar may show a different part of the coast than the charted shoreline, and low flat land may not show at all
Because the object's range changes with the gain setting
Because identification affects the speed of light
questions.explanation: A wooded hill behind the shore can paint as the coast, while a low spit may be missing. Matching shape and range patterns on chart and screen avoids a wrong fix.

questions.stem: At 10 knots you take the range to a headland dead ahead, and two minutes later the range to an island on the beam. What is the problem if both are plotted as one fix?
options: The ship has moved about 0.33 nm between readings, so the headland range is stale by about that much
The island range is stale by 0.33 nm and the headland range is correct
There is no problem, because radar ranges update automatically
The ship has moved about 3.3 nm
questions.explanation: 10 knots for 2 minutes is 10 × 2 ÷ 60 = 0.33 nm. A range to an object ahead or astern changes at nearly your full speed, while a range to an object abeam hardly changes. Read the fast-changing range as close as possible to the plotting time.

questions.stem: What is parallel indexing used for?
options: Measuring the wind speed from the clutter pattern
Calibrating the heading marker
Finding the radar's transmitted power
Watching cross-track error with a line on the radar screen parallel to the planned track
questions.explanation: A parallel index line is set parallel to the planned track at the distance a chosen object should pass. If the echo slides along the line, the ship is on track. It works best on a stabilised display.
